edges.relationship: Cooper identifies Genovese’s slavery scholarship as a formative influence on his comparative work on East Africa.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview, 2017 reprint:342 and 348/notes 11, 20, credits the American-South course taught by David Potter and names Genovese among the slavery historians who shaped him. The later French interview, 2022:45–46, calls Genovese the historian who most marked this work, especially plantation production relations and the world economy. The latter witness misdates Roll, Jordan, Roll as 1972; the reprint note 20 and existing publisher record give 1974. No new reading of Genovese’s books, formal mentorship or unqualified adoption of all his interpretations is claimed.

edges.relationship: Woodward’s history of the post-emancipation American South helped form Cooper’s comparative approach to African slavery.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2017 reprint:341–342 describes Potter’s course and Woodward’s book as part of the education that made Cooper’s dissertation comparative from the start. Note 12 identifies The Origins of the New South, 1877–1913 in a 1971 manifestation. The book is not newly read, and that citation date is not asserted as its first publication. Potter’s teaching remains distinct from Woodward’s reading influence.

edges.relationship: Cooper names David Brion Davis among the slavery historians who shaped his early scholarship.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2017 reprint:348 explicitly recalls formative slavery scholarship by Genovese, Davis and Emilia Viotti da Costa. Note 21 lists The Problem of Slavery in Western Culture (1966) and The Problem of Slavery in the Age of Revolution (1975). This is Cooper’s retrospective intellectual debt, not proof that both books predated his 1974 dissertation, formal supervision, or fresh reading of either original. Da Costa remains an equally named missing-endpoint lead.

edges.relationship: Cooper credits sustained reading of Marx with shaping his inquiry into capitalist transformation while testing theory against failed and contested transitions.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2017 reprint:341–344 describes increasing study of Marx, a particular rather than exclusive Marxist thread, and reciprocal testing of theory and historical evidence. Own 2022:46 specifies closer engagement with Capital between his first slavery book and From Slaves to Squatters. The 2000 essay:61–62 and 67/note 3 uses capital as a social relation and the colonial limits of primitive accumulation, citing the Moore/Aveling 1906 volume 1 colonization chapter. These readings retain resistance, contingency and other intellectual sources; the cited Capital edition is not independently reread.

edges.relationship: Cooper credits collaboration with Stoler for developing a research agenda on colonial societies through the interplay of historical inquiry and anthropology.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2017 reprint:343–344/notes 15–17 explains that similarly framed studies of East African and Sumatran agriculture led to shared conferences, the 1989 American Ethnologist papers and the jointly edited Tensions of Empire (1997). He describes theory and empirical work as mutually informative. Stoler is a collaborator with her own research, not Cooper’s formal teacher, sole origin of colonial studies, or author of every contribution. The 1989 and 1997 introduction bodies and Stoler’s monograph remain unread here; existing source metadata and group route are preserved.

edges.relationship: Cooper acknowledges learning from Foucault while rejecting the demand that historians all follow a cultural turn.
edges.evidence_note: Own French interview 2022:47 explicitly says he learned much from reading Foucault, then rejects compulsory disciplinary turns and the neglect of labour history. The witness supports a bounded acknowledged reading resource, with no named Foucault title, exclusive intellectual formation, or acceptance of every Foucauldian claim inferred. The French answers translate English email exchanges and were reviewed by Cooper.

edges.relationship: Cooper presents Du Bois as a resource for thinking about the changing relationship between social thought, political action and constraint.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview 2022:43–44 corrects the questioners’ suggestion of a continuous early debt: Cooper says full appreciation came years after his first article. He then explains Du Bois’s combination of contextual understanding and transformative action, relating the 1903 colour-line claim to later civil-rights and African-liberation struggles. This is later reflective uptake, not proof that Du Bois directly determined his earliest work or fresh reading of Du Bois’s originals. Historical claims remain Cooper’s.

edges.relationship: Cooper describes a shared concern with Goody to challenge histories that make Europe the sole driver of the world’s past.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview 2022:56–58, especially 57, responds to the Goody question by identifying a shared criticism of Eurocentric framing. Cooper describes the distinct Burbank–Cooper inter-imperial project, Eurasian focus and tension between comparison and connection. This is an explicitly supported comparison, not a claim of personal contact, causal influence, identical arguments or fresh reading of Goody’s books. Jane Burbank retains equal coauthorship despite lacking a full endpoint.

edges.relationship: Cooper questions Eley and Nield’s priority for discourse and micropolitics, asking how material structures, long-distance relations and varied political connections also shape class.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2000:60–67 praises the joint essay’s conciliatory effort and essential cultural insights while challenging its starting priorities and identity-centred definition of politics. Both Geoff Eley and Keith Nield are targets of one joint argument. Cooper seeks a dynamic relation between discourse and structures, not an economic reversal or dismissal of culture. His Mandela/Buthelezi examples remain his interpretation, not independently checked histories. The original Eley–Nield essay is not freshly read here; their selected joint reply is represented separately.

edges.relationship: With Nield, Eley answers Cooper that he overstates their differences and leaves the concepts of experience, actual structures and agency insufficiently questioned.
edges.evidence_note: Joint reply 2000:81–83 quotes Cooper’s political account, agrees on much of his description and on capitalism’s importance, then defends a provisional cultural starting point. The criticism is jointly Eley’s and Keith Nield’s, not sole authorship, and their agreement with Cooper’s concluding historical task is retained. Fresh selected 76–83 reading is distinct from the prior selected 81–86 record. Cooper’s 1995 Thompson essay is invoked by the reply but remains unread.

edges.relationship: Cooper sees a retrospective categorical difficulty in Thompson’s attempt to show how a working class made itself while assuming the class as its outcome.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2000:68/note 11 names The Making of the English Working Class (1963) as a parallel to constructivist arguments that begin from the later category and miss alternative affinities. This is a precise qualification, alongside the positive analogy to struggles against class formation at 62. It is not a wholesale rejection of Thompson, a fresh reading of The Making, or reuse of the separately unread 1995 retrospective.

edges.relationship: Cooper uses Chakrabarty’s distinction between abstract and real labour to analyze the continuing tension between general claims and workers’ particularity.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2000:62 and 67–68/note 4 explicitly takes up Chakrabarty’s distinction, naming Marx After Marxism: History, Subalternity and Difference (Meanjin 52, 1993:421–434). Cooper emphasizes that both general and specific registers can be useful in labour politics. This is a stated conceptual resource rather than agreement with every Chakrabarty argument or fresh reading of the 1993 original. It is distinct from the existing group account and from the 1989 Bengal book.

edges.relationship: Cooper uses James’s account of exploitation and transatlantic revolutionary mobilization to connect labour organization with political ideas across empires.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2000:63/note 7 at 68 attributes to James both the organization of Caribbean plantation labour and the movement of revolutionary news and claims. The note cites The Black Jacobins in its 1963 edition while the prose dates the original argument 1938. Cooper places Trouillot’s qualification beside James’s account; this is an argumentative use, not fresh reading or independent verification of James’s historical claims.

edges.relationship: Cooper uses Trouillot’s account of varied Haitian political imaginations to qualify a wholly Jacobin account of the revolution.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2000:63/note 7 at 68 explicitly contrasts the Jacobin current with other imaginations brought from Africa and redeployed in Haiti. James’s transatlantic account remains positively represented alongside this qualification. The note points to Trouillot’s 1995 book; the citation’s title wording is not taken as an alternative work. No fresh book reading or verification of every Haitian case is claimed.

edges.relationship: Cooper positively uses Eley and Blackbourn’s account of varied capitalist transitions alongside his criticism of Eley and Nield’s later class framework.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2000:62 praises Eley’s argument that non-English histories are particular processes of accumulation rather than failed copies of England. Note 3 at 67 identifies the jointly authored The Peculiarities of German History (1984). David Blackbourn retains coauthor credit; the prose’s specific praise of Eley does not remove Blackbourn’s joint authorship. The book is unread here, and this particular resource neither erases the reciprocal 2000 critique nor establishes wholesale personal formation.

edges.relationship: Brown credits his reading and exchanges with Mary Douglas with helping him interpret religion within distinctive social worlds.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2003 lecture:2–3 and 9 explicitly corrects a seminar-based transmission story: an electrifying 1968 tea was followed by reading Purity and Danger privately and the Natural Symbols manuscript while travelling. The later account of British social anthropology at 12–14 retains the limits of explaining holiness from outside. This is a concrete reading and conversational debt, not formal seminar attendance, exclusive formation, or fresh reading of Douglas’s books. The existing anthropology influence remains intact.

edges.relationship: Brown acknowledges Foucault’s friendship and writings as resources for his work on the self and sexual renunciation, while giving Hadot intellectual priority.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2003:2–3 describes the late 1980 Augustine/Cassian conversation and later informal encounters rather than seminars. At 13–14 Brown credits Hadot first, explains that Hadot drew him toward Foucault’s Care of the Self, and distinguishes their approaches. Own 2022:255/note 12 positively uses Les aveux de la chair, published posthumously in 2018, in reconsidering virginity as a bid for freedom. The later work cannot explain the 1988 book. Hadot’s stronger explicit debt is held for a missing endpoint; Foucault’s books and Brown’s complete memoir remain unread. The 2024 interview’s editorial Foucault claim is not treated as Brown’s own answer.

sources.citation: Peter Brown, Peter Brown and the Making of Late Antiquity (entretien avec Peter Brown), Anabases 36 (2022):245–257; online release 2 November 2024.

verification.note: Read complete original publisher interview 245–257 with bibliography,PDFleaves 2–14, plus metadata cover. The 17 leaf file has extra blank/divider material, not 17 pages of interview. Printed 2 November 2022 differs from online 2 November 2024. Momigliano/Marrou, Hadot, Patlagean, Pirenne, Gurevich, Rebillard and later students retain distinct roles and holds. Les aveux de la chair 2018 is later than The Body and Society 1988; no backward causal claim or fresh cited-book reading.

sources.title: Peter Brown, A Life of Learning, Haskins Lecture for 2003
sources.citation: Peter Brown, A Life of Learning, Charles Homer Haskins Lecture for 2003, ACLS Occasional Paper 55 (American Council of Learned Societies, 2003), 1–20.

verification.note: Read complete own lecture 1–20 in the original learned-society PDF,34 leaves; title, contents, biography and Oakley introduction separately identified. Named Douglas/Foucault encounters were informal, not seminars. Hadot’s prior, stronger debt and Momigliano’s mentorship remain explicit. No new cited-original or monograph reading, institutional universalization or independent historical validation.

sources.title: Frederick Cooper, interview with Iva Peša and Alicia Schrikker, 2017 reprint
sources.citation: Iva Peša and Alicia Schrikker, Lessons from African History: between the deep and the shallow ends of social theory and historical empiricism. Interview with Frederick Cooper, in Carolien Stolte and Alicia Schrikker, eds., World History – a Genealogy (Leiden University Press, 2017), 337–352; interview conducted December 2013, first published Itinerario 38:3 (2014), 7–18, doi:10.1017/S0165115314000497.

verification.note: Read the complete Cooper interview 337–352, including all 24 notes, in the public publisher ebook retained from the Library of Congress; exact shared PDF hash recorded privately without changing the frozen Goody files. These are reprint locators, not original journal pagination. Publisher metadata verifies editors and 2017 edition. Neither the complete 430 page book nor original 2014 journal manifestation was newly read. Own answers are distinguished from interviewer questions and editorial bibliography. Woodward 1971 is a cited manifestation, and Davis 1975/da Costa 1985 cannot be assumed to predate his 1974 dissertation.

sources.title: Guillaume Vadot and Étienne Bourel, interview with Frederick Cooper, 2022
sources.citation: Guillaume Vadot and Étienne Bourel, Le travail, les idées et la question sociale dans l’histoire contemporaine de l’Afrique. Entretien avec Frederick Cooper, Cahiers d’études africaines 245–246 (2022): 41–61.

verification.note: Read complete original journal PDF 41–61 with metadata cover, 22 leaves, from its publisher. English email exchanges December 2021–February 2022 were translated into French by Vadot and Bourel and reviewed by Cooper in February 2022. The interview corrects a question’s implied early Du Bois influence, names Genovese and Capital, acknowledges Foucault, and compares the Burbank–Cooper project with Goody without proving influence. Its erroneous 1972 Roll, Jordan, Roll date is distinguished from the 1974 record in the 2017 witness/existing publisher record. Historical and disciplinary generalizations remain attributed, not independently adjudicated.

loc_cooper_category_2000.note: Fresh complete original Cambridge journal PDF 60–68 read, including all 18 notes. This permitted publisher reading confirms the earlier full-article record without silently extending it to cited books. Cooper’s praise and criticism of the joint Eley–Nield essay coexist; positive Eley/Blackbourn resource, Chakrabarty distinction, James/Trouillot complementary uses, Marx and Thompson’s categorical difficulty retain exact notes and coauthor/edition limits. Political and historical examples are Cooper’s analyses, not fresh archival validation.

loc_eley_nield_reply_2000.note: Fresh selected 76–83 read in the original Cambridge PDF, especially the complete Cooper response 81–83 through the agreement with his concluding task. Eley and Keith Nield share all reply credit. Their objections to his alleged distancing, experience, structures and agency coexist with substantial agreement. Later Scott discussion on 83 is not reassigned to Cooper. Prior selected 81–86 record remains; no new full 76–87 reading or original Cooper 1995 essay reading.

ri189_brown_nyrb_interview.note: Complete displayed original publisher interview reread, especially the concluding anthropology answer and distinction between historical otherness and facile present-day analogy. Arjini’s introductory Foucault description remains editorial framing; Brown’s own 2003 lecture and 2022 interview supply the personal debt proposed separately. No audio, complete memoir, cited monograph or independent historical adjudication claimed.

rationale: Existing endpoints only; preserve named mediation, coauthorship, critical qualifications, edition and reading limits. All old graph records unchanged apart from append-only source reading notes. Tocqueville excluded as an owned dossier or newly read primary body, not as an existing resource endpoint in another historian’s own testimony. No new biographies, fields, life facts, chronology or dissertation analysis. OpenAlex remains paused.
